Preimplantation Genetic Diagnosis

By: Laura Byrne | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
High-tech genetic testing allows prospective parents to avoid passing life-threatening genetic conditions on to their children.

Unique Selling Point:
We are closer than ever to the idea of 'designer babies': fertility specialists and geneticists are helping prospective parents avoid passing on the potentially life-threatening genetic conditions they carry on to their children. For some parents, the knowledge of the conditions they carry comes only when they give birth to a child affected by the condition.

Summary:
Preimplantation Genetic Diagnosis (PGD) is a genetic testing procedure that allows parents to 'select' healthy embryos and avoid giving birth to children who either carry or are affected by hereditary genetic conditions. First, genetic material (a cheek swab) is taken from both parents (who may be carriers of a recessive genetic condition, or affected by a dominant one). This material is used to design a test unique to that couple. Then the couple undergoes ordinary IVF: eggs are harvested and fertilised. At about 8 days, the embryos are biopsied: one or two cells are removed, the DNA is extracted and compared against the test for the genetic condition. An embryo that is neither affected by the condition nor (preferably) carries it is then implanted. The remaining healthy embryos may be frozen and used for later pregnancies, or donated to other couples.
We have three wonderful case studies who have all battled different and terrible conditions, undergone PGD and had healthy babies.

Further information:
Case Study 1: Emma and Joe Hall
Joe Hall has a dominant genetic condition called bulbous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, which essentially means he was born without skin. He was the first child born in South Africa to survive this condition. When they wanted to have children, Emma and Joe were told to try conceiving naturally first. They fell pregnant twice but at 12 weeks in both cases, the foetus tested positive for the condition. These babies have a 60-70% chance of miscarriage and often die at birth, so the decision was taken to terminate both pregnancies. The Halls then used the samples from their 2 pregnancies to devise a test for the condition. They underwent 2 rounds of IVF but only harvested 3 eggs, of which only 1 was successfully fertilised. But on testing, it was found that the embryo did not have the condition. Riley was born in January 2016.

Case Study 2: Lomar and Shezanne (sp?) Breet
Lomar and Shezanne are both unwitting carriers of an autosomal recessive condition called AL6-CDG, one of several congenital disorders of glycolisation. They knew something was wrong with their first baby when he was born, but were already 22 weeks pregnant with their second when the genetic diagnosis was made. Their older children are now 8 and 5 but are quite severely impaired - Shezanne says the hardest thing is knowing they will never call her Mommy. AL6-CDG can cause low muscle tone, developmental delay, seizures, and digestive problems but only 54 people have been diagnosed with the condition and knowledge is scarce. While they were going through the process of diagnosing the condition, they were put in touch with Dr Lawrence Gobetz at VitaLab, and decided to undergo PGD. They were able to produce 4 normal embryos and implanted the first one last year, born on 18 January. They are now pregnant with another embryo from the same round of PGD.

Half-day producer and camera fee in Durban (Carol Albertyn-Christie and camera Rich Hamlock) for interviews with the Halls.

Press Release:


Reproduction is something we take for granted, but on a closer look, genetics can seem like a dangerous gamble. Seventy percent of us carry one or more genetic mutations, which can result in life-threatening or debilitating conditions for our children. But now a cutting-edge procedure called Preimplantation Genetic Diagnosis (PGD) offers the opportunity to stop some hereditary diseases in their tracks and remove them from the family tree forever.


Script:


UPSOUND: JOE HALL It’s a moral dilemma, if you think about passing this gene onto a child.
UPSOUND: LOMAR BREET When Lian was born, it was just turned upside down.
LINK: CLAIRE MAWISA Most of us take reproduction entirely for granted. Hundreds of thousands of healthy babies are born into the world daily. But on a closer glance, the lottery of genetics can seem like a dangerous gamble.
VO1: Your genetic makeup is determined by information contained in 23 pairs of chromosomes – half from mom, and half from dad. 70% of us carry a genetic mutation, like the one that caused Joe Hall’s rare skin condition.
UPSOUND: JOE HALL It’s as If the interlocking of the skin cells – it doesn’t interlock correctly. And that’s why you get uneven, flaky, dry patchy skin.
VO2: At birth, Joe’s skin came off, and his survival was touch and go.
UPSOUND: JOE HALL Because my skin is very soft, I would hurt myself and other kids don’t have that and you don’t understand what’s wrong with you. Infections can flare up in a matter of a couple of hours.
VO3: Joe’s condition is dominant, so he had a 50% chance of passing it onto his children. When he and his partner Emma decided to try for kids, they knew the road ahead would be difficult.
UPSOUND: EMMA HALL Everybody thinks it’s a natural thing to just have a baby. But we knew it wasn’t going to be something we could just do. The first doctor we went to was a dermatologist. And he said to us, with Joe’s condition, it’s a 50/50. And so try naturally, which we did.
VO4: At 12 weeks, the foetus tested positive for the mutation. Joe and Emma faced the likelihood that their baby would miscarry or die shortly after birth...or live to suffer as Joe did. They made the heart-wrenching decision to terminate.
UPSOUND: EMMA HALL The doctors then told us to try again. So we did try again. And we fell pregnant a few months later and same thing.
UPSOUND: JOE HALL I can imagine how hard it is to just go terminate a pregnancy that you don’t want, but one that you do want is – it is – I can’t describe it.
UPSOUND: EMMA HALL We went into a big depression. Joe and I changed completely. We lost each other I think for a long time.
VO5: It took a cutting edge procedure, Preimplantation Genetic Diagnosis, to provide the answer for Joe and Emma…and for Lomar and Suzanne Breet, who had no way of knowing they both carried a rare recessive mutation, until their first son Lian stopped breathing at five and a half months.
UPSOUND: SUZANNE BREET When we got the diagnosis it was devastating to us.
VO6: AL6-CDG is vanishingly rare, with only 54 people diagnosed worldwide. It causes a metabolic condition that left Lian with very low muscle tone, impaired vision, and cognitive underdevelopment. He will never live a normal life.
Recessive conditions don’t manifest unless both copies of a particular gene are faulty. Lomar and Suzanne are carriers: they each have one faulty gene. They had only a 25% chance of having an affected child.
UPSOUND: LOMAR BREET A lot of the guys said why not have more children. There’s 75% chance that you’re going to have children that are normal.
VO7: But their worst fears came true when their second child Ziani was diagnosed with the same condition.
UPSOUND LOMAR BREET It just felt like someone pulled the carpet from underneath you.
LINK: Lomar and Suzanne’s struggle with the error hidden deep in their genes is representative of what brings many couples to Preimplantation Genetic Diagnosis.
UPSOUND: DR JAYSEN KNEZOVITCH Preimplantation Genetic Diagnosis, or PGD, is the diagnosis of what we call single gene disorders. So these are disorders that are caused by a mutation in a single gene.
VO8: Dr Jaysen Knezovitch is the Managing Director of Genesis Genetics, which offers a range of reproductive genetic tests for prospective parents.
UPSOUND: DR JAYSEN KNEZOVITCH So really what PGD is, is basically looking to see whether an embryo is actually carrying that particular gene, the mutated gene, and therefore carrying that condition.
UPSOUND: DR LAWRENCE GOBETZ It’s been available worldwide nearly 25 years if not a little bit longer.
VO9: Fertility specialist Dr Lawrence Gobetz sees 10 to 15 PGD cases per year.
UPSOUND: DR LAWRENCE GOBETZ We can only really offer it currently to patients who know that they carry a genetic condition or have given birth to a child with a lethal genetic condition.
VO10: Genetic samples from each parent are sent to an overseas laboratory, where a unique test is designed for the couple’s specific mutation. The couple then undergoes in-vitro fertilisation.
UPSOUND: DR JAYSEN KNEZOVITCH Most PGD families don’t have fertility issues. The only reason that they’re visiting a fertility clinic is because those clinics have the ability to generate embryos outside the body. And by doing that, we obviously have access to the genetic information of the embryos.
VO11: The embryos are ‘grown’ in the laboratory for 5 days. A few cells are removed from each embryo, the DNA is extracted, amplified, and sent overseas to be compared against the family’s unique test with 98% accuracy. One or two unaffected embryos are then implanted.
Having a healthy child of their own was something Suzanne and Lomar couldn’t let go of.
UPSOUND: SUZANNE BREET We wanted a child to share life with and teach a child something.
VO12: The Breets produced five affected embryos and four unaffected carriers. After a successful implantation, Lomar Jnr was born.
UPSOUND SUZANNE BREET To be able to see a child look at you, is something that I’ve never had before. My children don’t look at me because they can’t see. And to hear him say mommy. That is something that I’ve never experienced before.
VO13: For Emma and Joe too, PGD offered a chance to overcome the genetic odds. But after punishing rounds of IVF, only three embryos survived long enough to be biopsied and tested.
UPSOUND: EMMA HALL The chances weren’t good that we were going to get a healthy baby from that.
VO14: But they finally got their break. One of the embryos was unaffected.
UPSOUND: EMMA HALL when we found out that she was healthy, that there was a healthy embryo, I think we just took a deep breath and I think smiled again.
VO15: In January 2016 Riley was born, and Joe’s condition was erased from the family tree.
UPSOUND: EMMA HALL I couldn’t even hold her because I was shaking so badly. But it was just – it was just a happy ending.
UPSOUND: JOE HALL It was such a good feeling to know that this child will come into this life and she won’t be affected by this horrible disease.
LINK: Currently, the technology exists to test 800 or more genetic conditions. So why aren’t we all getting our DNA thoroughly screened – just in case?
UPSOUND: DR JAYSEN KNEZOVITCH There are 6 billion places that we could potentially look to on the human genome, and when we’re doing tests like PGD we’re only looking in one place. So to look for a vast variety of genetic conditions or genetic traits would be virtually impossible.
UPSOUND: DR LAWRENCE GOBETZ Unless you know what you’re looking for, you cannot earmark in the laboratory what you’re going to test for. Eventually we will get to a level where every embryo will be chipped for all the genetic conditions that we do know of.
LINK: So what is stopping us from choosing hair colour, IQ or the athletic ability of our children…in short, creating designer babies?
UPSOUND: DR JAYSEN KNEZOVITCH Traits like IQ and height are the collective input of many genes within the genome. Things like athletic ability is not only the genetics that constitutes that trait. It’s also the environment in which one grows up.
UPSOUND DR LAWRENCE GOBETZ I think that you will always have those people that think are we playing God? At the end of the day we are using medical science to help desperate couples out there have a normal child.
LINK: Legal and ethical fears about genetic meddling aside, in South Africa, where the majority of the population struggles to access basic healthcare, this cutting edge procedure remains available to only a very few who can afford it.
UPSOUND: CLAIRE MAWISA This sounds very complicated and very expensive. How much does it cost?
DR LAWRENCE GOBETZ Patients are looking at somewhere between R80 and 90 000 for a cycle of treatment.
UPSOUND DR HELEN MALHERBE PGD is an extremely useful tool in our arsenal of screening. But it needs to be available for everybody.
VO16: Dr Helen Malherbe is the chair of Genetic Alliance South Africa.
UPSOUND: DR HELEN MALHERBE For the 85% of the population that don’t have access to medical aid, PGD and specialist services like that are completely unavailable.
VO17: One in 15 live births is affected by a congenital disorder, of which over 80% have genetic causes. 70% can be prevented, cured or ameliorated with adequate care. Yet South Africa has just 12 medical geneticists in three provinces.
UPSOUND: DR HELEN MALHERBE We’re only going to see significant reductions in our child mortality if we tackle the issue of congenital disorders. And there’s a real lack of political will to actually invest in the genetic services.
VO18: In this context, PGD seems like a faraway luxury. But for those who can afford it, cost, pain and stress fall away in the joy of holding a healthy baby.
UPSOUND: SUZANNE BREET I’m pregnant now with our last embryo and I’m not afraid now because I have seen the result.
UPSOUND: JOE HALL It’s given me that happiness of a family life. It’s given us the ability to not to have to gamble with genetics.


IN-STUDIO PROMO (10 SEC)
UPSOUND: Joe Hall: It’s a moral dilemma, if you think about passing this gene onto a child.
VO: A cutting edge technology allows parents to select genetic mutations out of their family trees forever.

TONIGHT PROMO (15 SEC)
UPSOUND: Suzanne [03:35:43] When we got the diagnosis it was devastating to us.
VO: Preimplantation Genetic Diagnosis offers families the chance to load the genetic dice in their favour.
UPSOUND: Lawrence: We are using medical science to help desperate couples out there have a normal child.

TONIGHT PROMO (15 SEC)
UPSOUND: Joe Hall: It’s given us the ability to not to have to gamble with genetics.
VO: Medical technology is putting the very alphabet of life at our fingertips.
UPSOUND Lawrence Gobetz: I think that you will always have those people that think are we playing God, or are we messing with nature?

One or two unaffected embryos are then implanted. Having a healthy child of their own was something Suzanne and Lomar couldn’t let go of. UPSOUND: SUZANNE BREET We wanted a child to share life with and teach a child something. VO12: The Breets produced five affected embryos and four unaffected carriers. After a successful implantation, Lomar Jnr was born. UPSOUND SUZANNE BREET To be able to see a child look at you, is something that I’ve never had before. My children don’t look at me because they can’t see. And to hear him say mommy. That is something that I’ve never experienced before. VO13: For Emma and Joe too, PGD offered a chance to overcome the genetic odds. But after punishing rounds of IVF, only three embryos survived long enough to be biopsied and tested. UPSOUND: EMMA HALL The chances weren’t good that we were going to get a healthy baby from that. VO14: But they finally got their break. One of the embryos was unaffected. UPSOUND: EMMA HALL when we found out that she was healthy, that there was a healthy embryo, I think we just took a deep breath and I think smiled again. VO15: In January 2016 Riley was born, and Joe’s condition was erased from the family tree. UPSOUND: EMMA HALL I couldn’t even hold her because I was shaking so badly. But it was just – it was just a happy ending. UPSOUND: JOE HALL It was such a good feeling to know that this child will come into this life and she won’t be affected by this horrible disease. LINK: Currently, the technology exists to test 800 or more genetic conditions. So why aren’t we all getting our DNA thoroughly screened – just in case? UPSOUND: DR JAYSEN KNEZOVITCH There are 6 billion places that we could potentially look to on the human genome, and when we’re doing tests like PGD we’re only looking in one place. So to look for a vast variety of genetic conditions or genetic traits would be virtually impossible. UPSOUND: DR LAWRENCE GOBETZ Unless you know what you’re looking for, you cannot earmark in the laboratory what you’re going to test for. Eventually we will get to a level where every embryo will be chipped for all the genetic conditions that we do know of. LINK: So what is stopping us from choosing hair colour, IQ or the athletic ability of our children…in short, creating designer babies? UPSOUND: DR JAYSEN KNEZOVITCH Traits like IQ and height are the collective input of many genes within the genome. Things like athletic ability is not only the genetics that constitutes that trait. It’s also the environment in which one grows up. UPSOUND DR LAWRENCE GOBETZ I think that you will always have those people that think are we playing God? At the end of the day we are using medical science to help desperate couples out there have a normal child. LINK: Legal and ethical fears about genetic meddling aside, in South Africa, where the majority of the population struggles to access basic healthcare, this cutting edge procedure remains available to only a very few who can afford it. UPSOUND: CLAIRE MAWISA This sounds very complicated and very expensive. How much does it cost? DR LAWRENCE GOBETZ Patients are looking at somewhere between R80 and 90 000 for a cycle of treatment. UPSOUND DR HELEN MALHERBE PGD is an extremely useful tool in our arsenal of screening. But it needs to be available for everybody. VO16: Dr Helen Malherbe is the chair of Genetic Alliance South Africa. UPSOUND: DR HELEN MALHERBE For the 85% of the population that don’t have access to medical aid, PGD and specialist services like that are completely unavailable. VO17: One in 15 live births is affected by a congenital disorder, of which over 80% have genetic causes. 70% can be prevented, cured or ameliorated with adequate care. Yet South Africa has just 12 medical geneticists in three provinces. UPSOUND: DR HELEN MALHERBE We’re only going to see significant reductions in our child mortality if we tackle the issue of congenital disorders. And there’s a real lack of political will to actually invest in the genetic services. VO18: In this context, PGD seems like a faraway luxury. But for those who can afford it, cost, pain and stress fall away in the joy of holding a healthy baby. UPSOUND: SUZANNE BREET I’m pregnant now with our last embryo and I’m not afraid now because I have seen the result. UPSOUND: JOE HALL It’s given me that happiness of a family life. It’s given us the ability to not to have to gamble with genetics. IN-STUDIO PROMO (10 SEC) UPSOUND: Joe Hall: It’s a moral dilemma, if you think about passing this gene onto a child. VO: A cutting edge technology allows parents to select genetic mutations out of their family trees forever. TONIGHT PROMO (15 SEC) UPSOUND: Suzanne [03:35:43] When we got the diagnosis it was devastating to us. VO: Preimplantation Genetic Diagnosis offers families the chance to load the genetic dice in their favour. UPSOUND: Lawrence: We are using medical science to help desperate couples out there have a normal child. TONIGHT PROMO (15 SEC) UPSOUND: Joe Hall: It’s given us the ability to not to have to gamble with genetics. VO: Medical technology is putting the very alphabet of life at our fingertips. UPSOUND Lawrence Gobetz: I think that you will always have those people that think are we playing God, or are we messing with nature?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): High-tech genetic testing allows prospective parents to avoid passing life-threatening genetic conditions on to their children.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We are closer than ever to the idea of 'designer babies': fertility specialists and geneticists are helping prospective parents avoid passing on the potentially life-threatening genetic conditions they carry on to their children. For some parents, the knowledge of the conditions they carry comes only when they give birth to a child affected by the condition.
metadata.Summary: Preimplantation Genetic Diagnosis (PGD) is a genetic testing procedure that allows parents to 'select' healthy embryos and avoid giving birth to children who either carry or are affected by hereditary genetic conditions. First, genetic material (a cheek swab) is taken from both parents (who may be carriers of a recessive genetic condition, or affected by a dominant one). This material is used to design a test unique to that couple. Then the couple undergoes ordinary IVF: eggs are harvested and fertilised. At about 8 days, the embryos are biopsied: one or two cells are removed, the DNA is extracted and compared against the test for the genetic condition. An embryo that is neither affected by the condition nor (preferably) carries it is then implanted. The remaining healthy embryos may be frozen and used for later pregnancies, or donated to other couples. We have three wonderful case studies who have all battled different and terrible conditions, undergone PGD and had healthy babies.
metadata.Further information: Case Study 1: Emma and Joe Hall Joe Hall has a dominant genetic condition called bulbous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, which essentially means he was born without skin. He was the first child born in South Africa to survive this condition. When they wanted to have children, Emma and Joe were told to try conceiving naturally first. They fell pregnant twice but at 12 weeks in both cases, the foetus tested positive for the condition. These babies have a 60-70% chance of miscarriage and often die at birth, so the decision was taken to terminate both pregnancies. The Halls then used the samples from their 2 pregnancies to devise a test for the condition. They underwent 2 rounds of IVF but only harvested 3 eggs, of which only 1 was successfully fertilised. But on testing, it was found that the embryo did not have the condition. Riley was born in January 2016. Case Study 2: Lomar and Shezanne (sp?) Breet Lomar and Shezanne are both unwitting carriers of an autosomal recessive condition called AL6-CDG, one of several congenital disorders of glycolisation. They knew something was wrong with their first baby when he was born, but were already 22 weeks pregnant with their second when the genetic diagnosis was made. Their older children are now 8 and 5 but are quite severely impaired - Shezanne says the hardest thing is knowing they will never call her Mommy. AL6-CDG can cause low muscle tone, developmental delay, seizures, and digestive problems but only 54 people have been diagnosed with the condition and knowledge is scarce. While they were going through the process of diagnosing the condition, they were put in touch with Dr Lawrence Gobetz at VitaLab, and decided to undergo PGD. They were able to produce 4 normal embryos and implanted the first one last year, born on 18 January. They are now pregnant with another embryo from the same round of PGD.
